overview.title: 📖 Overview: When Does Misuse (Me'ilah) Still Apply?
overview.subtitle: Meilah 2a–2b
overview.hebrewSource: קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים שֶׁשְּׁחָטָן בַּדָּרוֹם – מוֹעֲלִין בָּהֶן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Masechet Meilah opens mid-topic, assuming the reader knows that misusing consecrated property (me'ilah) requires bringing a guilt offering and repaying the value plus one-fifth. The mishna teaches that offerings of the most sacred order disqualified by an improper location or time of slaughter — south instead of north, night instead of day — remain subject to me'ilah if one derives benefit from them. The Gemara explains why every listed case is necessary, then states Rabbi Yehoshua's guiding principle: an offering that once had 'a period of fitness for the priests' to eat is no longer subject to me'ilah once disqualified, but one that never had such a window remains fully consecrated. The daf closes with a dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef about offerings that ascended the altar despite disqualification, and whether the mishna's me'ilah is by Torah law or only rabbinic law.

slides.title: 🔄 The Mishna's Mixed-Up Cases
slides.subtitle: Location and time errors that still leave an offering subject to me'ilah
rows: Should be slaughtered in the north
The more significant rite (collection) was correct
The more significant rite was wrong
Slaughtered by day, blood sprinkled by night (or reverse)
One of the two rites at the wrong time
Intent to eat/sprinkle beyond its time or place

callout.label: Why list them all?
callout.text: The Gemara shows each case is needed: without it, one might think that only the exact combination taught is included, and that a different mix of correct/incorrect rites would be 'as though strangled' and exempt from me'ilah.

slides.title: 📜 Rabbi Yehoshua's Principle
slides.subtitle: Did the offering ever have a moment when priests could eat it?

nodes.content: ❓ A sacrificial animal becomes disqualified. Is one liable for me'ilah if he benefits from it?
📏 Rabbi Yehoshua's rule: כׇּל שֶׁהָיָה לָהּ שְׁעַת הֶיתֵּר לַכֹּהֲנִים — did it ever have a period of fitness for the priests?

columns.label: Had a period of fitness
columns.content: It stayed overnight (notar), became impure, or left the courtyard — after the priests could already eat it. No me'ilah.

columns.label: Never had fitness
columns.content: Slaughtered/sprinkled outside its time or place, or by disqualified people — the priests could never eat it. Me'ilah applies.

nodes.content: 🎯 Once permitted to priests, an offering exits the category of items forbidden to everyone; if never permitted, it stays fully consecrated to God

callout.label: Key line:
callout.text: Me'ilah applies only to items that are entirely forbidden for human use — once priests could have eaten it, that status ends even if it is later disqualified for another reason.

slides.title: ⚖️ Rabba vs. Rav Yosef: If They Ascended, Must They Descend?
slides.subtitle: A disqualified offering that reached the altar — sacrifice it or remove it?

lines.speaker: Rabba
lines.text: אִם עָלוּ – יֵרְדוּ. If a disqualified offering ascended the altar, it must still descend and not be sacrificed.

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: אִם עָלוּ – לֹא יֵרְדוּ. Once it has ascended, it stays and may be sacrificed.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: This only applies according to Rabbi Shimon's view (Zevaḥim 84a) — Rabbi Yehuda agrees such offerings always descend, no dispute there.

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: I follow Rabbi Shimon plainly: once inside the courtyard and on the altar, it stays.

lines.speaker: Rabba
lines.text: Not so — Rabbi Shimon meant only cases like blood placed above vs. below the red line, where slaughter and collection were done properly. Here, slaughtering in the south is like strangling the animal — it never counts as valid slaughter, so it must descend.

callout.label: The stakes:
callout.text: If Rabba is right that it must descend, the mishna's ruling that one is liable for me'ilah becomes puzzling — how can something removed from the altar still carry Torah-level me'ilah?

slides.title: 🚫 Why Piggul Offerings Still Carry Me'ilah
slides.subtitle: Chutz lizmano and chutz limkomo are unfit for consumption anywhere — so why not exempt from me'ilah?

boxes.title: The Question
items: Slaughtered/sprinkled with intent to eat or sprinkle beyond its time or place
Unfit even for offerings of lesser sanctity
For what are they now 'fit'? Why treat them as still consecrated?

boxes.title: The Answer
items: הוֹאִיל וּמְרַצִּין לְפִיגּוּלִין — the blood's sprinkling still 'accepts' the offering into piggul status
Piggul only takes effect if all permitting factors (like blood sprinkling) were done properly
That significance shows the offering has not fully lost its consecrated status

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: An offering's ability to trigger piggul — a stringency — is itself proof that it retains enough sanctity to remain subject to me'ilah.

slides.title: 💰 Torah-Law Me'ilah vs. Rabbinic-Law Me'ilah
slides.subtitle: Resolving the difficulty with Rabba's opinion
slides.hebrewSource: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא לְרַבָּנַן? דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא מְשַׁלְּמִין חוֹמֶשׁ, דְּרַבָּנַן – לָא
slides.label: The resolution:
slides.text: According to Rabba, an offering slaughtered in the south must descend from the altar — so the mishna's me'ilah must be only by rabbinic law, not Torah law. The practical difference: Torah-law me'ilah requires repaying the principal plus an extra one-fifth; rabbinic-law me'ilah does not. The Gemara supports the idea of rabbinic me'ilah from Ulla citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: sacrificial animals that died are excluded from Torah-law me'ilah, yet are still subject to it by rabbinic decree — precisely so people will not casually derive benefit from animals that still look like ordinary offerings.

summary.principle: Me'ilah applies to consecrated items only as long as they never had — or, per Rabba, only when they cannot rely on having had — a moment of legitimate access; Rabbi Yehoshua's 'period of fitness for the priests' is the Torah-law dividing line, while the Sages extended me'ilah by rabbinic decree to protect against casual misuse even of animals that are, strictly, no longer consecrated.

flowSteps.content: 📖 Mishna: offerings of the most sacred order slaughtered/sprinkled in the wrong place or time — subject to me'ilah
❓ Why list every combination of north/south, day/night?
📏 Rabbi Yehoshua: did it ever have a 'period of fitness for the priests'? If yes → no me'ilah; if never → me'ilah applies

columns.content: 🚫 Piggul offerings still count — the blood's power to trigger piggul proves lingering sanctity
⚖️ Rabba: if ascended, it must descend — so mishna's me'ilah is only rabbinic

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Torah-law me'ilah requires the extra one-fifth payment; rabbinic-law me'ilah, invoked to prevent casual misuse, does not

quiz.q: According to the mishna, if offerings of the most sacred order were slaughtered in the south of the courtyard instead of the north, what is the halakha?
o: They are entirely exempt from me'ilah, like an animal that died
One who derives benefit from them is liable for me'ilah
They may be eaten by the priests
They must be burned immediately
quiz.e: The mishna states that despite the disqualification, one who derives benefit from such offerings is liable for misusing them (me'ilah).

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Yehoshua's general principle for determining whether a disqualified offering is subject to me'ilah?
o: Whether the animal was male or female
Whether it ever had a period of fitness for the priests to eat
Whether it was a sin offering or a burnt offering
Whether the disqualification happened inside or outside Jerusalem
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehoshua taught: if the offering had a period when priests could eat it before disqualification, there is no me'ilah; if it never had such a period, me'ilah applies.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara say an offering slaughtered with intent to eat it beyond its designated time (piggul) still remains subject to me'ilah, despite being unfit even for offerings of lesser sanctity?
o: Because it may still be redeemed for money
Because its blood sprinkling still renders it accepted for the purpose of piggul, showing it retains consecrated status
Because piggul offerings are eaten by non-priests
Because the mishna does not actually include this case
quiz.e: The Gemara explains: since the blood-sprinkling 'accepts' the offering into piggul status, and piggul only takes effect when the permitting factors were done correctly, this shows the offering has not entirely lost its sanctity.

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef regarding an offering disqualified in the courtyard that already ascended the altar?
o: Whether it may be eaten by non-priests
Whether it must descend from the altar or may remain and be sacrificed
Whether it is subject to piggul
Whether its blood may be poured on the ground
quiz.e: Rabba holds that if it ascended, it must still descend; Rav Yosef holds that once it ascended, it need not descend and may be sacrificed.

quiz.q: According to Rabba's opinion, since a disqualified offering slaughtered in the south must descend from the altar, how does the Gemara explain the mishna's ruling that one is liable for me'ilah?
o: The me'ilah in the mishna is only by rabbinic law, not Torah law
The mishna is discussing a different type of offering entirely
Rabba retracts his opinion in light of the mishna
The me'ilah applies only to the priest who performed the slaughter
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by saying the mishna's me'ilah is rabbinic in origin; Torah-law me'ilah requires paying an additional one-fifth, while rabbinic-law me'ilah does not.
